commentary.seminaVerbi:
This pair of texts binds identity to imitation. A people becomes “chosen” not by ethnic insulation but by an enacted style of life; the proof of belonging is behavior that exceeds reciprocity. Psychologically, it is a demand to refuse the easy coherence of “us” against “them,” and to build the self on a harder axis: fidelity when instinct wants revenge, generosity when the body wants safety.

The command to love enemies is not sentiment but a re-training of attention. It breaks the addiction to mirrored emotions and recruits a larger model of reality: a world where goods are given without moral sorting. The self that can pray for an enemy is no longer organized around injury; it converts hostility into a disciplined practice of freedom.

Semina Verbi: the Stoic cosmopolis (Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius) similarly grounds ethical expansion in likeness to a rational order beyond tribal impulse. Mahayana Buddhism’s metta and bodhisattva vow aim at nonselective goodwill, even toward harm-doers; speculation: “perfection” here resembles the maturation of compassion beyond preference. In the Bhagavad Gita, acting without attachment to outcome loosens the grip of retaliation and reward. Confucian ren, extending care outward by deliberate cultivation, parallels the idea that moral excellence is formed, not merely felt.
commentary.excursus:
Deuteronomy sells a romance of mutual choosing, but it reads like a contract signed under a watchful eye. “This day” is a deadline: obey with all your heart, all your soul, or discover what your heart and soul are worth. The seduction is status. You are promised to be “higher than all nations,” lifted into holiness, which is just another word for separation. Desire is recruited as patriotism; dread keeps it in place.

Matthew doesn’t soften that pressure; he turns it inward until it becomes total. Love your enemies is not kindness but conquest of the reflex. You must take the hatred aimed at you, metabolize it, and return something clean, not because the enemy deserves it but because you are being remade into “children” who mimic a Father indifferent in his generosity. Sun and rain fall on everyone; your feelings don’t get a vote.

“Be perfect” is the most violent line here: not moral improvement but the demand for an unbroken self, no private exceptions, no permitted resentment. Deuteronomy offers elevation through obedience; Matthew demands a love that erases the boundary between friend and foe. Holiness becomes not superiority over other nations but superiority over your own nervous system. The promised reward is not peace; it is resemblance. That is both the longing and the terror.
commentary.synthesis: God’s election creates a people whose distinctiveness is measured by likeness to his indiscriminate goodness. Holiness is proven by enemy-directed love that refuses reciprocity as its standard.

gospel.text: Matthew extends the covenant ethic past tribal boundary-markers: the Father’s rule is displayed in non-selective beneficence, so filial resemblance requires a non-reciprocal social posture. The argument is comparative—ordinary courtesies toward kin and peers are morally inert—so the commanded excess functions as the distinctive sign of the kingdom.

reading.text: Deuteronomy binds identity to enacted allegiance: the people’s “walk” is not self-fashioning but the public shape of belonging. The promised “higher” status is teleological—aimed at producing a visible holiness that terminates in God’s reputation, not Israel’s self-congratulation.

marginalia.text: “This day”: law as immediate pressure, not archive; totalizing claim on heart/soul.
“Chosen” framed as consent; obedience cast as walking, not mere compliance.
Mutual election: divine choosing answers human choosing; “peculiar” marks separation by possession.
Elevation “higher” is liturgical—“to his…glory”—status converted into doxology; holiness is the intended output.
A counterfeit corollary: “hate thy enemy” smuggled in beside the command to love.
Three verbs against retaliation—love/do/pray—enemy redefined as object of deliberate action.
Meteorology as theology: indiscriminate sun/rain unmasks merit as a false criterion.
Reward logic exposes the baseline: reciprocal love requires no conversion; “publicans” are the control group.
“Therefore”: perfection is the conclusion of enemy-love, not an abstract ideal; measure is the Father.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: God, eternal Father, turn our hearts back to you, so that, consecrated to your service, we may seek nothing but you, the one thing necessary, and devote ourselves to the practice of works of mercy. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer:
Let us pray:

After First Vespers of Sunday or of solemnities that fall on Sunday:

Keep us, Lord, through this night, and grant that tomorrow, as the new day dawns, the celebration of Sunday may fill us with the joy of the resurrection of your Son. Who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

After Vespers of solemnities that do not fall on Sunday:

Visit, Lord, this room; drive far from it the snares of the enemy. Let your holy angels dwell here and keep us in peace, and may your blessing remain always with us. Through Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Compline

lines: This day the Lord thy God hath commanded thee to do these commandments and judgments: and to keep and fulfil them with all thy heart, and with all thy soul.
Thou hast chosen the Lord this day to be thy God, and to walk in his ways and keep his ceremonies, and precepts, and judgments, and obey his command.
And the Lord hath chosen thee this day, to be his peculiar people, as he hath spoken to thee, and to keep all his commandments:
And to make thee higher than all nations which he hath created, to his own praise, and name, and glory: that thou mayst be a holy people of the Lord thy God, as he hath spoken.
readings.heading: A reading from the Book of Deuteronomy

lines: You have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thy enemy.
But I say to you, Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you:
That you may be the children of your Father who is in heaven, who maketh his sun to rise upon the good, and bad, and raineth upon the just and the unjust.

For if you love them that love you, what reward shall you have? do not even the publicans this? The publicans... These were the gatherers of the public taxes: a set of men, odious and infamous among the Jews, for their extortions and injustice.
And if you salute your brethren only, what do you more? do not also the heathens this?
Be you therefore perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect.
